Entry: The entry point tells Webpack where to start resolving dependencies. It's the root module that Webpack uses to build the dependency graph. Multiple entry points are supported for multi-page apps.
Output: Output configuration tells Webpack where to emit the bundled files and how to name them. The path and filename properties are required. Content hashes enable long-term caching.
Loaders: Loaders allow Webpack to process files other than JavaScript by transforming them into valid modules. They are defined in the module.rules array and process right-to-left through a chain.
Plugins: Plugins extend Webpack's capabilities by performing optimizations, asset management, and environment injection. They are added to the plugins array and hook into the compilation lifecycle.
Mode: Webpack supports three modes: development, production, and none. Production mode enables optimizations like minification and tree-shaking. Development mode enables fast incremental builds and source maps.
Webpack 5 Features: Webpack 5 introduced built-in asset modules (replacing file-loader/url-loader), module federation, persistent caching, and better code splitting. Many older loaders are no longer needed.

Babel: Babel transpiles modern ES6+ JavaScript into backwards-compatible versions. The @babel/preset-env preset handles syntax transformation based on target browsers.
CSS/SASS: CSS and SASS loaders transform stylesheets into JavaScript modules. The chain of loaders processes right-to-left, typically sass-loader -> css-loader -> style-loader.
TypeScript: TypeScript is compiled via ts-loader or babel-loader with @babel/preset-typescript. ForkTsCheckerWebpackPlugin runs type checking in a separate process for faster builds.
Images & Fonts: Webpack 5 asset modules handle images, fonts, and other media files. The 'asset' type automatically inlines small files as base64 and emits larger ones as separate files.

HtmlWebpack: HtmlWebpackPlugin simplifies creation of HTML files that automatically include all Webpack bundles. It supports templating, minification, and cache-busting.
MiniCssExtract: MiniCssExtractPlugin extracts CSS into separate files instead of inlining them in JavaScript. This improves caching and parallel loading. Use it in production for better performance.
DefinePlugin: DefinePlugin creates global constants at compile time, useful for injecting environment variables. Values are evaluated as code expressions, so strings need JSON.stringify.
ProgressPlugin: ProgressPlugin reports build progress to the console during compilation. It's useful in CI environments and for monitoring slow builds during development.

Code Splitting: Code splitting breaks bundles into smaller chunks loaded on demand, reducing initial load time. SplitChunksPlugin handles shared module extraction automatically.
Tree Shaking: Tree shaking eliminates dead code by analyzing ES module import/export statements. It requires 'sideEffects': false in package.json and production mode to work correctly.
Minification: TerserWebpackPlugin minifies JavaScript by removing whitespace, renaming variables, and eliminating dead code. It runs automatically in production mode but can be customized.
Persistent Caching: Webpack 5 persistent caching stores compilation results to disk, dramatically speeding up subsequent builds. Set cache.type to 'filesystem' and provide a version or name.
Bundle Analysis: Bundle analysis tools visualize the composition of output bundles, helping identify large dependencies and opportunities for code splitting.

Dev/Prod: Separate Webpack configs for development and production allow different optimizations. A common config merged via webpack-merge avoids duplication across environments.

const { merge } = require('webpack-merge');
module.exports = (env) => merge(commonConfig, env.prod ? prodConfig : devConfig);
Multiple Configs: Webpack supports exporting an array of configurations for building multiple bundles in a single run, useful for libraries or multi-page applications.
Env Variables: Environment variables can be passed via CLI using --env and accessed in the config function. DefinePlugin injects them into application code at compile time.

HMR: Hot Module Replacement updates modules in the browser without a full page reload. It preserves application state during development for a faster feedback loop.
Proxy: Dev server proxy forwards API requests to a backend server during development, avoiding CORS issues. It supports path rewriting, HTTPS, and WebSocket proxying.
Live Reload: Live reload automatically refreshes the browser when files change. It is enabled by default in webpack-dev-server and works with watch mode for rapid development iteration.

Host Config: Module Federation allows multiple separate Webpack builds to share code and components at runtime. The host application consumes remotes and can share dependencies as singletons.
Remote Config: The remote application exposes components via ModuleFederationPlugin. It specifies which modules are exposed and what dependencies are shared with the host.
Shared Dependencies: Shared dependencies prevent multiple instances of the same library from loading. The singleton option ensures only one instance exists, and eager loads critical dependencies.

Custom Loaders: Custom loaders transform source files by implementing a function that receives the source and returns the modified output. Loaders run in a pipeline from right to left.
Custom Plugins: Custom plugins hook into Webpack's compilation lifecycle using the apply method and tap into compiler hooks for custom behavior.
Web Workers: Webpack supports Web Workers out of the box. Worker files can be bundled separately and instantiated with the standard Worker constructor.
PWA Support: Webpack can generate service workers and manifest files for Progressive Web Apps using WorkboxPlugin. It precaches static assets and enables offline functionality.

Caching: Webpack uses content hashes in filenames to enable long-term caching. The [contenthash] placeholder generates unique hashes based on file contents, so only changed files get new URLs.
Long-term Caching: Long-term caching strategies separate vendor code from application code so vendors change less frequently. Module IDs should be deterministic for stable chunk hashes.
